claim: Fear extinction is defined as a lessening of conditioned fear responses following extinction training, during which subjects are exposed to repetitive presentations of conditioned stimuli (CS) alone.
source: Fear extinction is defined as a lessening of conditioned fear responses following extinction training, during which subjects are exposed to repetitive presentations of conditioned stimuli (CS) alone (Pavlov, 1927; Bouton, 1988; Myers and Davis, 2007; Nader et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on fear extinction.

claim: Previous studies have provided numerous lines of evidence for the inhibition mechanism of fear extinction by which extinction training produces a new memory that inhibits the original fear memory stored in the lateral amygdala (LA).
source: Previous studies have provided numerous lines of evidence for the inhibition mechanism of fear extinction by which extinction training produces a new memory that inhibits the original fear memory stored in the lateral amygdala (LA) (Maren and Quirk, 2004; LeDoux, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the inhibition mechanism.

claim: The neural circuits underlying the inhibition mechanism of fear extinction have been identified in the prefrontal cortex, the basolateral amygdala, the LA, and intercalated neurons (ITC) of the amygdala.
source: The neural circuits underlying the inhibition mechanism of fear extinction have been identified in the prefrontal cortex, the basolateral amygdala, the LA, and intercalated neurons (ITC) of the amygdala (Milad and Quirk, 2002; Chhatwal et al., 2005; Herry et al., 2008; Likhtik et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2009; Amano et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies identifying these neural circuits.

claim: Strong evidence is available for the existence of the erasure mechanism through which a fear memory encoded in the LA is erased.
source: In contrast, strong evidence is also available for the existence of the erasure mechanism through which a fear memory encoded in the LA is erased (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972; Lin et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2007; Dalton et al., 2008; Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the erasure mechanism.

claim: Whether the original fear memory is inhibited or erased after extinction is still a subject of debate.
source: However, whether the original fear memory is inhibited or erased after extinction is still a subject of debate (Quirk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation indicating ongoing debate in the field.

claim: The inhibition mechanisms were studied and characterized at molecular and cellular levels mostly using single-session extinction training.
source: Intriguingly, the inhibition mechanisms were studied and characterized at molecular and cellular levels mostly using single-session extinction training (Milad and Quirk, 2002; Chhatwal et al., 2005; Herry et al., 2008; Likhtik et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2009; Amano et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using single-session extinction training.

claim: The erasure mechanism has been supported by previous studies using both single- and multiple-session extinction training.
source: In contrast, the erasure mechanism has been supported by previous studies using both single- and multiple-session extinction training (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972; Lin et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2007; Dalton et al., 2008; Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using different extinction training protocols.

claim: NMDA receptor activity in the LA has been reported to be involved selectively in single-session extinction training, but not subsequent relearning of extinction.
source: Furthermore, NMDA receptor activity in the LA has been reported to be involved selectively in single-session extinction training, but not subsequent relearning of extinction (Laurent et al., 2008; Laurent and Westbrook, 2008, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on NMDA receptor involvement.

claim: Prefrontal activity has been shown to be required for the recall of initial extinction training, but not gradual extinction over days.
source: Prefrontal activity has been shown to be required for the recall of initial extinction training, but not gradual extinction over days (Lebrón et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on prefrontal activity requirements.

claim: Single- and multiple-session extinction may involve different mechanisms in distinct neural circuits.
source: Thus, these previous studies suggest that single- and multiple-session extinction may involve different mechanisms in distinct neural circuits.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the preceding discussion of differential involvement of neural mechanisms.

claim: The infralimbic cortex (IL) is thought to be involved in suppressing conditioned fear outputs via its connectivity with the amygdala inhibitory neurons when extinction is recalled.
source: The infralimbic cortex (IL) is thought to be involved in suppressing conditioned fear outputs via its connectivity with the amygdala inhibitory neurons (Sotres-Bayon and Quirk, 2010; Quirk and Mueller, 2008), when extinction is recalled (Quirk et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on IL function.

claim: CS-evoked activities of IL neurons have been shown to appear during extinction recall after single-session extinction training.
source: Accordingly, CS-evoked activities of IL neurons have been shown to appear during extinction recall after single-session extinction training (Milad and Quirk, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating IL neuronal activity.

claim: Rats displayed robust freezing to the CS after fear conditioning, and conditioned fear responses progressively decreased over the three extinction sessions.
source: Rats displayed robust freezing to the CS after fear conditioning, and conditioned fear responses progressively decreased over the three extinction sessions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Single unit activities of a total of 72 neurons in the IL of 19 rats were recorded stably across the entire behavioral training.
source: Single unit activities of a total of 72 neurons in the IL of 19 rats were recorded stably across the entire behavioral training (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data on neuronal recordings referenced in supplementary figures.

claim: In the successful extinction recall group, strong excitatory activities of the IL appeared during post-Ext1.
source: In the successful extinction recall group (which included rats with lower freezing than the upper 99% confidence interval of freezing in post-Ext1; n = 14 rats; black in Figure 1C), strong excitatory activities of the IL appeared during post-Ext1 (F4,220 = 3.346, p=0.0319, p<0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. Hab, Repeated measures one-way ANOVA followed by Newman-Keuls post-test; black in Figure 1E,F), consistent with a previous report (Milad and Quirk, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal activity data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The transient appearance of IL neuronal activity quickly disappeared during the subsequent sessions.
source: Intriguingly, this transient appearance of neuronal activity quickly disappeared during the subsequent sessions (p>0.05 for post-Ext2, post-Ext3 vs. Hab; Figure 1E,F) and even during the Ext2 (black in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference in later sessions.

claim: In the poor extinction recall group, CS-evoked activities of IL neurons were largely unchanged throughout conditioning, subsequent extinction training sessions, and recall test.
source: In contrast, in the poor extinction recall group (which included rats with higher freezing than the upper 99% confidence interval of freezing in post-Ext1; n = 5 rats; gray in Figure 1C), CS-evoked activities of IL neurons were largely unchanged throughout conditioning, subsequent extinction training sessions, and recall test (F4,60 = 0.2742, p=0.7918, Repeated measures one-way ANOVA; gray in Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant changes.

claim: The transient increase in IL neuronal activity is only found in single-session extinction training but not in multiple-session extinction training.
source: These findings indicate that the transient increase in IL neuronal activity is only found in single-session extinction training but not in multiple-session extinction training.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of IL activity across different extinction sessions.

claim: A subpopulation of neurons in the basal nucleus of the amygdala (Ba) exhibits CS-evoked activities only when extinction is recalled after single-session extinction training.
source: It has been shown that a subpopulation of neurons in the basal nucleus of the amygdala (Ba), which is reciprocally connected with the IL, exhibits CS-evoked activities only when extinction is recalled after single-session extinction training (Herry et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study characterizing Ba neurons.

claim: A total of 130 neurons in the Ba of 27 rats were recorded stably across the entire behavioral training.
source: A total of 130 neurons in the Ba of 27 rats were recorded stably across the entire behavioral training (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data on neuronal recordings.

claim: Two distinct subpopulations of Ba neurons of 'fear neurons' and 'extinction neurons' were found.
source: As previously described (Herry et al., 2008), we found two distinct subpopulations of Ba neurons of 'fear neurons' and 'extinction neurons'.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and comparison to prior literature.

claim: 'Fear neurons' exhibited strong excitatory responses to the CS when conditioned fear was recalled after fear conditioning.
source: 'Fear neurons' (n = 8 neurons from 6 rats; 6.15% of recorded cells and 22.86% of CS-responsive cells; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) exhibited strong excitatory responses to the CS when conditioned fear was recalled after fear conditioning (χ2 = 14, p=0.0073, p<0.05 for post-Cond vs. Hab, Friedman test followed by Dunn's test; red in Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal activity data.

claim: 'Fear neurons' lost the activities after extinction training and remained unresponsive to CS in subsequent extinction training.
source: These 'fear neurons' lost the activities after extinction training (p>0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. Hab; Figure 2D), consistent with a previous study (Herry et al., 2008), and remained unresponsive to CS in subsequent extinction training (p>0.05 for post-Ext2, post-Ext3 vs. Hab).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and comparison to prior literature.

claim: 'Extinction neurons' did not show CS-evoked activities when conditioned fear was recalled after fear conditioning, but exhibited strong excitatory activities to the CS when extinction was recalled after single-session extinction training.
source: 'Extinction neurons' (n = 6 neurons from 6 rats; 4.62% of recorded cells and 17.14% of CS-responsive cells; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) did not show CS-evoked activities when conditioned fear was recalled after fear conditioning, but exhibited strong excitatory activities to the CS when extinction was recalled after single-session extinction training (χ2 = 10.67, p=0.0306, p<0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. Hab, Friedman test followed by Dunn's test; blue in Figure 2C,D), consistent with the previous finding (Herry et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The CS-evoked activities of 'extinction neurons' disappeared when extinction was recalled after additional extinction training.
source: Consistent with IL experimental results, the CS-evoked activities of 'extinction neurons' disappeared when extinction was recalled after additional extinction training (p>0.05 for post-Ext2, post-Ext3 vs. Hab; Figure 2D) and even during the Ext2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference in later sessions.

claim: 'Extinction neurons' in the Ba no longer reflect the low fear state especially after multiple-session extinction training.
source: These findings suggest that 'extinction neurons' in the Ba no longer reflect the low fear state especially after multiple-session extinction training and further confirm the results obtained with the IL.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of extinction neuron activity across sessions.

claim: Ba neurons synapse onto ITC cells, which are known to be GABAergic neurons.
source: Ba neurons synapse onto ITC cells, which are known to be GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of amygdala circuitry.

claim: ITC neurons further synapse onto central amygdala (CeA) neurons, which are the major output neurons of the amygdala.
source: ITC neurons further synapse onto central amygdala (CeA) neurons, which are the major output neurons of the amygdala.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of amygdala circuitry.

claim: Ba-ITC synapses are potentiated after single-session extinction training.
source: It has been shown that Ba-ITC synapses are potentiated after single-session extinction training (Amano et al., 2010), and this potentiation presumably leads to the inhibition of CeA neurons and, hence, fear outputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating synaptic potentiation.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio of AMPA EPSCs in the single-session extinction training group was significantly reduced compared to naïve controls.
source: The paired-pulse ratio of AMPA EPSCs in the single-session extinction training group was significantly reduced compared to naïve controls (χ2 = 8.419, p=0.0381, p<0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. naïve, Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's test; Figure 3C), whereas it returned to the level of naïve controls after additional extinction training (p>0.05 for post-Ext2, post-Ext3 vs. naïve; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The AMPA/NMDA EPSC ratio at Ba-ITC synapses was significantly enhanced after single-session extinction training but decreased with further extinction training.
source: Similarly, the AMPA/NMDA EPSC ratio at Ba-ITC synapses was significantly enhanced after single-session extinction training (χ2 = 14.25, p=0.0065, p<0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. naïve, post-Cond, Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's test; Figure 3D), but decreased with further extinction training (p<0.05 for post-Ext2, post-Ext3 vs. post-Ext1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Both the pre- and post-synaptic functions at Ba-ITC synapses, which are transiently enhanced after single-session extinction training, return to baseline after further extinction training.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that both the pre- and post-synaptic functions at Ba-ITC synapses, which are transiently enhanced after single-session extinction training, return to baseline after further extinction training.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined pre- and post-synaptic data.

claim: Postsynaptic functions at IN-PN synapses are known to be decreased after fear conditioning and to be enhanced after single-session extinction training.
source: Postsynaptic functions at IN-PN synapses are known to be decreased after fear conditioning and to be enhanced after single-session extinction training (Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on IN-PN synaptic function.

claim: The amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) was decreased after fear conditioning and enhanced after single-session extinction training.
source: The amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) was decreased after fear conditioning (χ2 = 46.92, p<0.0001, p<0.05 for post-Cond vs. naïve, Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's test) and enhanced after single-session extinction training (p<0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. naïve; Figure 4B,C), consistent with a previous finding (Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The enhancement in mIPSC amplitudes disappeared after multiple-session extinction training, and mIPSC amplitudes in the multiple-session extinction training group were not significantly different from those in naïve controls.
source: As expected, the enhancement in mIPSC amplitudes disappeared after multiple-session extinction training, and mIPSC amplitudes in the multiple-session extinction training group were not significantly different from those in naïve controls (p>0.05 for post-Ext2, post-Ext3 vs. naïve).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference.

claim: mIPSC frequency decreased following fear conditioning and returned to baseline after extinction.
source: mIPSC frequency decreased following fear conditioning and returned to baseline after extinction (χ2 = 17.93, p=0.0013, p<0.05 for post-Cond vs. naïve; p>0.05 for post-Ext1, post-Ext2, post-Ext3 vs. naïve, Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's test; Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Local inhibition in the LA is no longer present after multiple-session extinction training.
source: Thus, local inhibition in the LA is also no longer present after multiple-session extinction training.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mIPSC data showing return to baseline.

claim: An increase in the surface expression of GABAA receptors has been suggested to underlie the enhancement of mIPSC amplitudes in the LA after single-session extinction training.
source: An increase in the surface expression of GABAA receptors has been suggested to underlie the enhancement of mIPSC amplitudes in the LA after single-session extinction training (Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on GABAA receptor expression.

claim: The surface expression of the β2 and γ2 subunits of GABAA receptors increased after single-session extinction training.
source: The surface expression of the β2 (χ2 = 10.37, p=0.0030, Kruskal-Wallis test; Figure 5B) and γ2 (χ2 = 8.149, p=0.0253, Kruskal-Wallis test; Figure 5C) subunits of GABAA receptors increased after single-session extinction training, respectively (p<0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. post-Cond, Dunn's test, Figure 5B; p<0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. post-Cond, Dunn's test, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of biochemical data.

claim: The β2 and γ2 subunits of GABAA receptors return to baseline relative to the level in the post-Cond group after multiple-session extinction training.
source: Whereas, these subunits of GABAA receptors return to baseline relative to the level in the post-Cond group after multiple-session extinction training (p<0.05 for post-Ext3 vs. post-Ext1, p>0.05 for post-Ext3 vs. post-Cond, Dunn's test, for both β2 and γ2 subunits; Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of biochemical data.

claim: The expression levels of cadherin did not change with conditioning and subsequent extinction.
source: The expression levels of cadherin did not change with conditioning and subsequent extinction (χ2 = 1.164, p=0.7887, Kruskal-Wallis test, Figure 5B; χ2 = 0.6045, p=0.9109, Kruskal-Wallis test, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant changes.

claim: Changes in surface expression of GABAA receptors play a major role in regulating the inhibitory tone in the LA during and after single- and multiple-session extinction training.
source: Thus, the enhanced surface expression of the GABAA receptor subunits observed after single-session extinction training appeared to be no longer present after multiple-session extinction training, suggesting that changes in surface expression of GABAA receptors play a major role in regulating the inhibitory tone in the LA during and after single- and multiple-session extinction training.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of GABAA receptor expression changes.

claim: Fear conditioning induces potentiation at LA synapses, a cellular substrate of fear memory.
source: Fear conditioning induces potentiation at LA synapses, a cellular substrate of fear memory (Rogan et al., 1997; McKernan and Shinnick-Gallagher, 1997), whereas extinction training elicits erasure or depotentiation at LA synapses, thereby leading to reduced fear outputs (Lin et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2007; Dalton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating synaptic potentiation and depotentiation.

claim: Extinction training elicits erasure or depotentiation at LA synapses, thereby leading to reduced fear outputs.
source: Fear conditioning induces potentiation at LA synapses, a cellular substrate of fear memory (Rogan et al., 1997; McKernan and Shinnick-Gallagher, 1997), whereas extinction training elicits erasure or depotentiation at LA synapses, thereby leading to reduced fear outputs (Lin et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2007; Dalton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating depotentiation.

claim: T-LA synaptic efficacy was enhanced following fear conditioning.
source: T-LA synaptic efficacy, indicated by the slope of input-output curve, was enhanced following fear conditioning (χ2 = 24.84, p<0.0001, p<0.005 for post-Cond vs. naïve, Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's test; Figure 6C,D), as previously described (Kim et al., 2007; Hong et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Single-session extinction training produced a decrease in T-LA synaptic efficacy relative to the conditioned group, being indistinguishable from naïve controls.
source: Single-session extinction training produced a decrease in T-LA synaptic efficacy relative to the conditioned group, being indistinguishable from naïve controls (p<0.005 for post-Ext1 vs. post-Cond, p>0.05 for post-Ext1 vs. naïve; Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: After additional extinction training, T-LA synaptic efficacy tended to decrease further but T-LA synaptic efficacy in the three extinction groups was not significantly different from each other.
source: After additional extinction training, T-LA synaptic efficacy tended to decrease further but T-LA synaptic efficacy in the three extinction groups was not significantly different from each other (p>0.05 for post-Ext2, post-Ext3 vs. post-Ext1; Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant differences.

claim: A depotentiation of conditioning-induced potentiation at T-LA synapses appears to be present throughout multiple-session extinction training.
source: Thus, a depotentiation of conditioning-induced potentiation at T-LA synapses appears to be present throughout multiple-session extinction training, suggesting that the persistent erasure mechanism accounts for extinguished fear even after multiple-session extinction training.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of T-LA synaptic efficacy across sessions.

claim: D-Sap infusion after single-session extinction training significantly impaired extinction recall relative to the B-Sap-infused group.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Likhtik et al., 2008), D-Sap infusion after single-session extinction training significantly impaired extinction recall relative to the B-Sap-infused group (U = 34.5, p=0.0090, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: D-Sap infusion resulted in a significant reduction in the number of ITC neurons relative to the B-Sap-infused group after single-session extinction training.
source: Accordingly, D-Sap infusion resulted in a significant reduction in the number of ITC neurons relative to the B-Sap-infused group (U = 11, p=0.0006, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 7C), while it did not affect the number of cells in the adjacent CeA (U = 11, p=0.3095, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cell count data.

claim: D-Sap infusion after multiple-session extinction training did not significantly impair extinction recall relative to the B-Sap-infused group.
source: In contrast, D-Sap infusion after multiple-session extinction training did not significantly impair extinction recall relative to the B-Sap-infused group (U = 141.5, p=0.9793, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 7D), even with a significant reduction in the number of ITC neurons relative to the B-Sap-infused group (U = 11, p=0.0006, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 7E), without any changes in the number of neurons in the adjacent CeA (U = 15, p=0.6991, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral and cell count data.

claim: A post-extinction ablation of ITC cells is no longer effective in impairing extinction recall after multiple-session extinction training.
source: Together, these findings suggest that a post-extinction ablation of ITC cells is no longer effective in impairing extinction recall after multiple-session extinction training.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ITC lesion data showing differential effects.

claim: Extinction mechanisms change when single-session extinction training is repeated.
source: In this study, we have shown that extinction mechanisms change when single-session extinction training is repeated.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: Inhibition of the original fear memory, which is governed by the prefrontal cortex and ITC neurons, is predominant during single-session extinction training but subsides after that.
source: Inhibition of the original fear memory, which is governed by the prefrontal cortex and ITC neurons, is predominant during single-session extinction training but subsides after that, whereas the original fear memory encoded in the LA is erased when single-session extinction training is repeated (see Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is the main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The original fear memory encoded in the LA is erased when single-session extinction training is repeated.
source: Inhibition of the original fear memory, which is governed by the prefrontal cortex and ITC neurons, is predominant during single-session extinction training but subsides after that, whereas the original fear memory encoded in the LA is erased when single-session extinction training is repeated (see Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is the main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The inhibition of original fear memory copes immediately and transiently with CSs that are no longer fearful, whereas fear memory erasure works in a more persistent manner when extinguished CSs become habituated.
source: According to this scenario, the inhibition of original fear memory copes immediately and transiently with CSs that are no longer fearful, whereas fear memory erasure works in a more persistent manner when extinguished CSs become habituated.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The return of fear after multiple session extinction indicates that the original memory is still present in some structures or circuits.
source: An obvious solution to this problem is to distinguish cellular erasure in a given structure (that is, amygdala) from brain-wide erasure of the entire memory. The return of fear after multiple session extinction simply indicates that the original memory is still present in some structures or circuits.
evidence: This claim is a logical inference addressing the apparent contradiction between erasure and fear return.

claim: Fear memory traces are distributed in multiple brain regions, such as the prefrontal cortex and associated cortical areas.
source: Consistently, previous findings have shown that fear memory traces are distributed in multiple brain regions, such as the prefrontal cortex and associated cortical areas (Frankland et al., 2004; Corcoran and Quirk, 2007; Do-Monte et al., 2015b; Senn et al., 2014; Kitamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on distributed fear memory.

claim: Erased cellular traces at amygdala synapses after multiple session extinction may be reconstructed through a metaplastic mechanism.
source: Alternatively, erased cellular traces at amygdala synapses after multiple session extinction may be reconstructed through a metaplastic mechanism (Lee et al., 2013; Maren, 2015; Clem and Schiller, 2016).
evidence: This claim is a speculative alternative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Correlates for the inhibition mechanism for fear extinction, which are active during single-session extinction training, abruptly disappear after multiple-session extinction training.
source: Correlates for the inhibition mechanism for fear extinction, which are active during single-session extinction training, abruptly disappear after multiple-session extinction training (see Figures 1–5).
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from multiple experiments shown in Figures 1-5.

claim: Cell-type specific ablation of ITC cells, which impairs extinction recall after single-session extinction training, is no longer effective after multiple-session extinction training.
source: Likewise, cell-type specific ablation of ITC cells, which impairs extinction recall after single-session extinction training, is no longer effective after multiple-session extinction training (see Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ITC lesion experiment data shown in Figure 7.

claim: A correlate for the erasure mechanism (that is, depotentiation at LA synapses) persists with single and multiple-session extinction training.
source: By contrast, a correlate for the erasure mechanism (that is, depotentiation at LA synapses) persists with single and multiple-session extinction training (see Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the T-LA synaptic efficacy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Manipulation of LA synaptic depotentiation using GluA2-3Y attenuates fear extinction persistently with single and multiple-session extinction training.
source: Consistently, manipulation of LA synaptic depotentiation using GluA2-3Y (a peptide blocker of GluA2-containing AMPAR internalization) attenuates fear extinction persistently with single and multiple-session extinction training (Kim et al., 2007; Dalton et al., 2008; Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using GluA2-3Y manipulation.

claim: Molecular and structural markers (GluA1 & 2, mGluR1 and dendritic spines) of the erasure mechanism persist throughout multiple-session extinction training.
source: Additionally, molecular and structural markers (GluA1 & 2, mGluR1 and dendritic spines) of the erasure mechanism persist throughout multiple-session extinction training (Kim et al., 2007; Hong et al., 2011; Lai et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on molecular and structural markers.

claim: As multiple-session extinction training proceeds, the original fear memory is transiently inhibited in the early phase of extinction training whereas the erasure of fear memory persistently supports all the phases of extinction training.
source: Together, all these findings can be nicely fitted into one scenario that as multiple-session extinction training proceeds, the original fear memory is transiently inhibited in the early phase of extinction training whereas the erasure of fear memory persistently supports all the phases of extinction training (see Figure 8).
evidence: This is the main integrative conclusion drawn from all experimental results and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The inhibition mechanisms in various brain regions (that is, prefrontal cortex, Ba, LA and ITC) disappear in concert after multiple-session extinction training.
source: It is quite striking that the inhibition mechanisms in various brain regions (that is, prefrontal cortex, Ba, LA and ITC) disappear in concert after multiple-session extinction training (see Figures 1–5).
evidence: This claim summarizes the coordinated disappearance of inhibition mechanisms across brain regions.

claim: Ba 'extinction neurons', LA interneurons and ITC cells receive excitatory inputs from the IL.
source: Indeed, Ba 'extinction neurons', LA interneurons and ITC cells receive excitatory inputs from the IL (Herry et al., 2008; Amano et al., 2010; Rosenkranz and Grace, 2002, but see also Likhtik et al., 2005) (see Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on IL connectivity.

claim: The IL orchestrates the inhibition mechanisms in various brain regions via synaptic connections.
source: Based on these functional connections, we propose that the IL orchestrates the inhibition mechanisms in various brain regions via synaptic connections; hence, the disappearance of the IL-based inhibition mechanism leads to the loss of other inhibition mechanisms.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the connectivity data and experimental results.

claim: Individual IL cells were found that were similar to 'extinction neurons' in the Ba.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found individual IL cells that were similar to 'extinction neurons' in the Ba (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The disappearance of IL responsiveness to the CS after multiple-session extinction training may lead to the complete loss of the inhibition mechanisms.
source: Thus, the disappearance of IL responsiveness to the CS after multiple-session extinction training may lead to the complete loss of the inhibition mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the IL orchestration hypothesis.

claim: Ba 'extinction neurons' send inputs to IL neurons, and inactivation of this connection impairs fear extinction.
source: Ba 'extinction neurons' send inputs to IL neurons, and inactivation of this connection impairs fear extinction (Senn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Ba-IL connectivity.

claim: The latencies of CS-responses of Ba 'extinction neurons' are faster than those of IL 'extinction neurons'.
source: Furthermore, the present study has shown that the latencies of CS-responses of Ba 'extinction neurons' are faster than those of IL 'extinction neurons' (see the legend in Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis referenced in a figure legend.

claim: Fear memory inhibition represents a transient mechanism for the early phase of extinction training.
source: The present results suggest that fear memory inhibition represents a transient mechanism for the early phase of extinction training contrary to what most researchers studying extinction believe.
evidence: This is a main conclusion that challenges prevailing views in the field.

claim: CS-evoked activity of IL neurons may be required for triggering depotentiation of conditioning-induced synaptic potentiation at LA synapses.
source: For example, CS-evoked activity of IL neurons, which is known to underlie extinction recall, may also indeed be required for triggering depotentiation of conditioning-induced synaptic potentiation at LA synapses: prefrontal neurons send excitatory drive onto LA principal neurons and proper depolarization is required for depotentiation induction at LA synapses (Likhtik et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative reinterpretation of IL function supported by citations.

claim: The IL plays a critical role during extinction training.
source: A recent study has indeed shown that the IL also plays a critical role during extinction training (Do-Monte et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Multiple-session extinction training in animals better represents human exposure therapy that requires repeated treatment for days or weeks.
source: The present findings have far-reaching implications for the clinical application of basic research based on fear extinction because multiple-session extinction training in animals better represents human exposure therapy that requires repeated treatment for days or weeks (Foa et al., 1999; Nader et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature and represents a translational inference.

claim: Enhanced prefrontal activity and reduced amygdala activity are observed during exposure therapy in humans, whereas the enhanced prefrontal activity returns to baseline and the reduced amygdala activity persists after the therapy.
source: In fact, from a mechanistic point of view, exposure therapy in humans shows similar patterns to the results obtained in the present study. Enhanced prefrontal activity and reduced amygdala activity are observed during the therapy, whereas the enhanced prefrontal activity returns to baseline and the reduced amygdala activity persists after the therapy (see Figure 1 of Quidé et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a human neuroimaging study showing parallel findings.

claim: Previous findings concerning the inhibition mechanisms of fear extinction may be more applicable to the early phase of exposure therapy, resulting in only transient effects.
source: Thus, previous findings concerning the inhibition mechanisms of fear extinction may be more applicable to the early phase of exposure therapy, resulting in only transient effects, whereas a more persistent therapeutic effect of exposure therapy could result from targeting the cellular and molecular changes after multiple-session extinction training.
evidence: This is a speculative clinical implication based on the experimental findings.

claim: The present findings set a new standard for drug development to treat fear/anxiety-related disorders.
source: Taken together, the present findings set a new standard for drug development to treat fear/anxiety-related disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the translational impact of the findings.

claim: The apparent extinction of the inhibition mechanisms during multiple-session extinction training may be mediated by erasure or second round of inhibition.
source: Ironically, just as extinction has been proposed to be mediated by both erasure (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972) and inhibition (Bouton, 1988), the apparent extinction of the inhibition mechanisms may also be mediated by erasure or second round of inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism underlying the disappearance of inhibition mechanisms.
